description: Machine credentials and secrets that commonly leak into server/application logs: JWTs, AWS access keys, PEM private-key blocks, vendor API tokens with documented fixed prefixes (GitHub, GitLab, Google, Slack, Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, npm, Anthropic), HTTP Authorization Bearer/Basic credentials, connection-string passwords, and generic key=secret assignments. These tokens are high-entropy and prefix/context-anchored, so the detectors are precise. Replacements are structurally valid for their kind but provably INVALID (they embed the literal REDACTED sentinel, which every detector's `safe` recognises) so a leaked credential is scrubbed before upload, not merely flagged.
notes: All replacements carry the literal 'REDACTED' sentinel (base64url-safe, so even a fake JWT or AKIA key stays shape-valid). Every detector therefore uses safe='REDACTED' for idempotency — the rare real secret that itself contains the substring 'redacted' is simply left alone, which is acceptable.

Vendor-token detectors anchor on the published prefix + length (e.g. ghp_/gho_/ghu_/ghs_/ghr_ + 36, github_pat_ 22_59, glpat- 20, AIza 35, xox[baprs]-, sk_/rk_ live|test, SK + 32 hex, SG. 22.43, npm_ 36, sk-ant-). Their fakes KEEP the prefix so the log still reads like 'a <vendor> token was here'. Publishable/identifier variants are excluded on purpose: Stripe pk_, Twilio AC… account SID.
Bearer credentials that are JWTs are shaped back into a fake JWT; opaque tokens and Basic credentials become an opaque REDACTED token. AWS access keys keep the AKIA/ASIA + 20-char shape.

Entropy-only secrets with NO stable prefix (e.g. an AWS secret access key, generic 32-hex API keys) are deliberately NOT pattern-matched here — they would over-match in logs; the generic key=secret assignment detector plus a downstream review layer cover those.

The generic key=secret assignment detector is the broadest here (matches api_key/secret/token/password/...= '<value>'); it lives in this opt-in profile precisely because that breadth is unwanted by default.

conn-string-password is space-tolerant and semicolon-tolerant only inside connection-string context (a neighbouring ';key=' on the line). A bare 'password=' in free prose or on a command line keeps the whitespace-terminated form, so an ordinary log sentence loses the credential and nothing else. Over-redaction of the surroundings is a product failure of its own: the user, host, database and command shape are the diagnostic value that survives redaction.

Quoted value branches require a delimiter after the closing quote. A quoted run that cannot close can always shorten itself to a shorter valid run, and a value opening with a doubled quote is exactly that shape, so the alternative to the requirement is a placeholder followed by the rest of the credential. Sending that text to an eat-to-end branch over-redacts the remainder of the line and leaks nothing, which is the trade this profile makes every time the two conflict.

Length ceilings on a CONTEXT run (a neighbouring key name, a URL userinfo username) are leaks, not limits: past the ceiling the match fails and the credential ships, or the value stops being bounded and eats the neighbour. Ceilings on the VALUE are a different matter and are not used either, since a credential has no maximum length worth guessing.

detectors.name: private-key-block
detectors.description: PEM-encoded private key block (RSA/EC/DSA/OpenSSH/PGP/encrypted). The whole block, including the armor lines, is replaced.

detectors.name: jwt
detectors.description: JSON Web Token. The 'eyJ' prefix is base64url of '{"' — a reliable JWT header signal — followed by header.payload(.signature).

detectors.name: aws-access-key
detectors.description: AWS access key id (AKIA long-term / ASIA temporary): a vendor-defined prefix + 16 uppercase-alnum chars, so essentially no false positives.

detectors.name: github-token
detectors.description: GitHub access token: a documented gh{p,o,u,s,r}_ prefix (personal/oauth/user-to-server/server-to-server/refresh) followed by 36 base62 chars.

detectors.name: github-pat-fine
detectors.description: GitHub fine-grained personal access token: github_pat_ + 22 chars + '_' + 59 chars.

detectors.name: gitlab-pat
detectors.description: GitLab personal access token: glpat- + 20 chars.

detectors.name: google-api-key
detectors.description: Google API key: the fixed AIza prefix + 35 chars.

detectors.name: slack-token
detectors.description: Slack token (xoxb/xoxp/xoxa/xoxr/xoxs- bot/user/app/refresh/config prefix).

detectors.name: slack-webhook
detectors.description: Slack incoming-webhook URL; the team/channel/token path segments are the secret (the host is kept).

detectors.name: stripe-secret-key
detectors.description: Stripe secret/restricted key (sk_/rk_ live or test). Publishable pk_ keys are intentionally NOT matched (not secret).

detectors.name: twilio-api-key
detectors.description: Twilio API key SID (SK + 32 hex). The AC… account SID is an identifier, not a secret, and is not matched.

detectors.name: sendgrid-key
detectors.description: SendGrid API key (SG. + 22 chars + '.' + 43 chars).

detectors.name: npm-token
detectors.description: npm access token: npm_ + 36 base62 chars.

detectors.name: anthropic-key
detectors.description: Anthropic API key (sk-ant- prefix).

detectors.name: auth-bearer
detectors.description: Credential following an HTTP 'Bearer ' scheme (Authorization header / curl logs). The scheme word is kept; the token is redacted.

detectors.name: auth-basic
detectors.description: base64 credential following an HTTP 'Basic ' scheme (it decodes to user:password).

detectors.name: conn-string-url-password
detectors.description: Password embedded in a URL's userinfo, e.g. postgres://user:PASS@host. Only the password (between ':' and '@') is redacted; a host:port with no '@' is left alone. THE USERNAME RUN IS UNBOUNDED. A ceiling on it is a leak rather than a limit: a userinfo username longer than the ceiling fails the whole match, and the password after it then ships verbatim. Nothing about a long username makes the credential behind it less of a credential, and a token, an account id or a URL-encoded principal all routinely run past any figure that looks generous.

detectors.name: conn-string-password
detectors.description: Credential value in a `key=value` assignment: `Password=`, `pwd=`, `passwd=`, Azure `AccountKey=`, `AccessKey=`, `ClientSecret=`, `SharedAccessSignature=`, and the hyphen and underscore spellings of each. Only the value is replaced: the key, the separator and every neighbouring option survive, because the user, host, database and command shape are the diagnostic value that has to outlive redaction. AN OPTIONAL IDENTIFIER PREFIX in front of the key catches `SecretAccessKey=` and `AwsSecretAccessKey=`, which a bare word boundary misses because no boundary exists between a lowercase letter and an uppercase one; that form is the SECRET half of an AWS key pair. The key must still sit immediately before the `=`, so `MyPasswordPolicy=`, `PasswordExpiryDays=`, `LastPasswordChange=` and `accesskeyid=` (the PUBLIC half of the pair) are not matched. FIVE VALUE FORMS, tried in order. A QUOTED value, in either quote, ends at its closing quote and understands a doubled quote as an escaped one. That closing quote must be followed by a delimiter or the end of the line, and the requirement is what stops a partial redaction: a quoted run that cannot close can always SHORTEN itself to a shorter valid run, and a value opening with a doubled quote is exactly that shape, so without the requirement the empty pair matches, the placeholder lands, and the credential behind it ships. A value in CONNECTION-STRING CONTEXT (the key is preceded by `;key=`, or another `;key=` follows on the line) runs to a `;` that is followed by a plausible next key, or to the end of the line, so spaces and embedded semicolons inside the value are covered. Then the two UNTERMINATED-QUOTE fallbacks, which eat to the end of the line rather than leave half a credential behind. Last, a BARE value ends at whitespace: it consumes interior quotes, since an apostrophe is an ordinary character to a command interpreter and `password=don't` must go whole, but it backs off a trailing quote so the surrounding quoting stays balanced. THE KEY RUN IS UNBOUNDED AND UNICODE-AWARE, and both halves are load-bearing. A ceiling on the length of the following key name means a longer neighbour key is not recognised as a key at all, the value eats to the end of the line, and the neighbour the detector exists to preserve dies with it. `\w` is ASCII-only in JavaScript, so a key spelt in any other script would fail the same way; the Unicode property classes and the `u` flag are what keep an ordinary non-English log from over-redacting. THE VALUE MAY NOT BEGIN WITH WHITESPACE, which is a cost rule rather than a matching one: the separator run in front of it is variable-length, so without the rule a long run of spaces after an `=` would offer the engine one start position per space and each of them would re-scan the line. Every value form starts on a non-space character anyway, so nothing is lost. THE FLAG-TOKEN GUARD keeps the connection-string branch off a command line: `;word=` can appear anywhere, including inside a quoted argument, so without the guard `--account-key=K; --metadata "env=prod;tier=1"` would run the value across the rest of the command. A run that reaches whitespace followed by a flag sigil stops there.

detectors.name: json-credential-value
detectors.description: Credential value in a JSON object member ("sessionpassword":"...", "password":"...", "apiToken": "...", "client_secret":"..."). A JSON body carries no '=', so neither connection-string detector can see it, and a REST or RPC result body is exactly where a session credential travels in full. THE KEY MUST END WITH THE CREDENTIAL WORD: the closing quote sits immediately after it, so a key that merely CONTAINS one is untouched ("passwordExpiryDays", "passwordPolicy", "tokenCount", "lastPasswordChange", and "accesskeyid", the PUBLIC half of an AWS key pair). The key list is WIDER than the connection-string one (token, secret, credential, passphrase are added) because a quoted key immediately before a ':' is a field name rather than a word in a sentence, which is a far stronger signal than the same word in free prose; widening the '=' list to match would drag those words into prose. Only the value BETWEEN the quotes is replaced, so the object stays parseable JSON. JSON escapes are honoured, so a '\\"' inside a value cannot end the match early and leave a tail of the credential behind. An UNQUOTED value (a JSON number, true/false/null) is NOT matched: the engine replaces a matched span with a placeholder and cannot re-quote it, so redacting one would emit invalid JSON. Object and array values are not matched either: finding their end needs balanced counting, which a regex cannot do.

detectors.name: secret-assignment
detectors.description: Generic 'key = value' secret assignment (api_key/secret/token/password/...): the value (>=8 chars) is redacted. Broadest detector here — opt-in by design.
